claim: Ceramides are central intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism.
source: Ceramides are central intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism that also function as potent messengers in stress signaling and apoptosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ceramide function in sphingolipid metabolism.

claim: Ceramides function as potent messengers in stress signaling and apoptosis.
source: Ceramides are central intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism that also function as potent messengers in stress signaling and apoptosis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ceramide signaling roles.

claim: Light-induced alterations in the lateral packing of caCers lead to marked differences in their metabolic conversion by sphingomyelin synthase.
source: Combining atomic force microscopy on model bilayers with metabolic tracing studies in cells, we demonstrate that light-induced alterations in the lateral packing of caCers lead to marked differences in their metabolic conversion by sphingomyelin synthase and glucosylceramide synthase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AFM and metabolic tracing studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Light-induced alterations in the lateral packing of caCers lead to marked differences in their metabolic conversion by glucosylceramide synthase.
source: Combining atomic force microscopy on model bilayers with metabolic tracing studies in cells, we demonstrate that light-induced alterations in the lateral packing of caCers lead to marked differences in their metabolic conversion by sphingomyelin synthase and glucosylceramide synthase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AFM and metabolic tracing studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Changes in metabolic rates of caCers are instant and reversible over several cycles of photoswitching.
source: These changes in metabolic rates are instant and reversible over several cycles of photoswitching.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reversible metabolic conversion over multiple light cycles.

claim: Sphingolipids contribute to mechanical stability, cell signaling and molecular sorting in eukaryotic cells.
source: Sphingolipids are unusually versatile membrane components in eukaryotic cells that contribute to mechanical stability, cell signaling and molecular sorting (Holthuis et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Holthuis et al., 2001.

claim: Sphingolipids derive from the addition of various polar head groups to ceramide.
source: They derive from the addition of various polar head groups to ceramide, a hydrophobic molecule containing saturated or trans-unsaturated acyl chains linked to a serine backbone (Wegner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wegner et al., 2016.

claim: Ceramide is a hydrophobic molecule containing saturated or trans-unsaturated acyl chains linked to a serine backbone.
source: They derive from the addition of various polar head groups to ceramide, a hydrophobic molecule containing saturated or trans-unsaturated acyl chains linked to a serine backbone (Wegner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wegner et al., 2016.

claim: Intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism influence cell proliferation, cell death, migration, stress adaptation, immune responses and angiogenesis.
source: Intermediates of sphingolipid metabolism, notably sphingosine, ceramide and their phosphorylated derivatives, influence a multitude of physiological processes, including cell proliferation, cell death, migration, stress adaptation, immune responses and angiogenesis (Hannun and Obeid, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hannun and Obeid, 2018.

claim: Imbalances in sphingolipid metabolism are linked to major human diseases.
source: Consequently, imbalances in sphingolipid metabolism are linked to major human diseases (Ogretmen, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ogretmen, 2018.

claim: Sphingomyelin (SM) and glycosphingolipids (GSLs) are the main sphingolipid classes in mammals.
source: Sphingomyelin (SM) and glycosphingolipids (GSLs) are the main sphingolipid classes in mammals (Koval and Pagano, 1991; D'Angelo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koval and Pagano, 1991 and D'Angelo et al., 2013.

claim: SM forms a concentration gradient along the secretory pathway.
source: SM forms a concentration gradient along the secretory pathway and influences cellular cholesterol homeostasis to sustain vital physical properties of the plasma membrane, where SM and Chol are enriched (Slotte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Slotte, 2013.

claim: SM influences cellular cholesterol homeostasis to sustain vital physical properties of the plasma membrane.
source: SM forms a concentration gradient along the secretory pathway and influences cellular cholesterol homeostasis to sustain vital physical properties of the plasma membrane, where SM and Chol are enriched (Slotte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Slotte, 2013.

claim: SM and cholesterol are enriched at the plasma membrane.
source: SM forms a concentration gradient along the secretory pathway and influences cellular cholesterol homeostasis to sustain vital physical properties of the plasma membrane, where SM and Chol are enriched (Slotte, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Slotte, 2013.

claim: The hydrolysis of plasma membrane SM by sphingomyelinases generates ceramide.
source: The hydrolysis of plasma membrane SM by sphingomyelinases generates ceramide, which mediates several stress responses including cell cycle arrest, senescence and apoptosis (Adada et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Adada et al., 2016.

claim: Ceramide generated by sphingomyelinases mediates cell cycle arrest, senescence and apoptosis.
source: The hydrolysis of plasma membrane SM by sphingomyelinases generates ceramide, which mediates several stress responses including cell cycle arrest, senescence and apoptosis (Adada et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Adada et al., 2016.

claim: SM synthase (SMS) catalyzes the transfer of phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine (PC) onto ceramide, yielding SM and diacylglycerol (DAG).
source: SM biosynthesis is mediated by SM synthase (SMS), an enzyme catalyzing the transfer of phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine (PC) onto ceramide, yielding SM and diacylglycerol (DAG).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic mechanism of SMS.

claim: Mammals contain two SMS isoforms: SMS1 and SMS2.
source: Mammals contain two SMS isoforms, namely SMS1, responsible for bulk production of SM in the Golgi lumen, and SMS2, serving a role in regenerating SM from ceramides released by sphingomyelinases on the cell surface (Huitema et al., 2004; Yamaoka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huitema et al., 2004 and Yamaoka et al., 2004.

claim: SMS1 is responsible for bulk production of SM in the Golgi lumen.
source: Mammals contain two SMS isoforms, namely SMS1, responsible for bulk production of SM in the Golgi lumen, and SMS2, serving a role in regenerating SM from ceramides released by sphingomyelinases on the cell surface (Huitema et al., 2004; Yamaoka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huitema et al., 2004 and Yamaoka et al., 2004.

claim: SMS2 serves a role in regenerating SM from ceramides released by sphingomyelinases on the cell surface.
source: Mammals contain two SMS isoforms, namely SMS1, responsible for bulk production of SM in the Golgi lumen, and SMS2, serving a role in regenerating SM from ceramides released by sphingomyelinases on the cell surface (Huitema et al., 2004; Yamaoka et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huitema et al., 2004 and Yamaoka et al., 2004.

claim: Studies in mice revealed roles for SMS1 and SMS2 in inflammation, atherosclerosis and diabetes.
source: Besides their biological potential as cross-regulators of the pro-apoptotic factor ceramide and mitogenic factor DAG, studies in mice revealed roles for SMS1 and SMS2 in inflammation, atherosclerosis and diabetes (Mitsutake et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mitsutake et al., 2011, Li et al., 2011, and Liu et al., 2009.

claim: GSLs are synthesized by the sequential action of Golgi-resident glycosyltransferases.
source: Conversely, GSLs are synthesized by the sequential action of Golgi-resident glycosyltransferases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GSL biosynthesis.

claim: Glycosyltransferases conjugate ceramide to a specific carbohydrate from a sugar nucleotide or onto a ceramide-conjugated carbohydrate chain.
source: These enzymes conjugate ceramide to a specific carbohydrate from a sugar nucleotide (e.g. UDP-glucose, UDP-galactose), or onto a ceramide-conjugated carbohydrate chain, giving rise to a large variety of structurally and functionally divergent compounds (D'Angelo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to D'Angelo et al., 2013.

claim: GSLs are dispensable for cell survival.
source: While GSLs are dispensable for cell survival, they are key to cell-cell communication and collectively required for mammalian development (D'Angelo et al., 2013; Yamashita, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to D'Angelo et al., 2013 and Yamashita, 2000.

claim: GSLs are key to cell-cell communication and collectively required for mammalian development.
source: While GSLs are dispensable for cell survival, they are key to cell-cell communication and collectively required for mammalian development (D'Angelo et al., 2013; Yamashita, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to D'Angelo et al., 2013 and Yamashita, 2000.

claim: Manipulation of cellular lipid pools by altering expression of metabolic enzymes is a slow process.
source: Manipulation of cellular lipid pools by altering expression of metabolic enzymes is a slow process, allowing cells to mount an adaptive response that dampens functional impact.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the limitations of genetic manipulation approaches.

claim: Altering expression of metabolic enzymes allows cells to mount an adaptive response that dampens functional impact.
source: Manipulation of cellular lipid pools by altering expression of metabolic enzymes is a slow process, allowing cells to mount an adaptive response that dampens functional impact.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cellular adaptive responses.

claim: Lipid metabolic networks are highly interconnected.
source: The fact that lipid metabolic networks are highly interconnected also makes it difficult to prove that the direct product of a specific enzyme is the actual effector.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lipid metabolism.

claim: Chemical dimerizers and optogenetic approaches allow researchers to manipulate lipid levels more rapidly.
source: Chemical dimerizers and optogenetic approaches allow researchers to manipulate lipid levels more rapidly, but their application often requires extensive protein engineering and is largely restricted to soluble lipid-metabolic enzymes or transfer proteins (Jain et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jain et al., 2017.

claim: Chemical dimerizers and optogenetic approaches often require extensive protein engineering and are largely restricted to soluble lipid-metabolic enzymes or transfer proteins.
source: Chemical dimerizers and optogenetic approaches allow researchers to manipulate lipid levels more rapidly, but their application often requires extensive protein engineering and is largely restricted to soluble lipid-metabolic enzymes or transfer proteins (Jain et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jain et al., 2017.

claim: Caged lipids carry a photo-labile protecting group that blocks their biological activity until the active lipid is released with a flash of light.
source: Another method to rapidly increase lipid supply involves the use of caged lipids. These compounds carry a photo-labile protecting group that blocks their biological activity until the active lipid is released with a flash of light (Kim et al., 2016; Höglinger et al., 2014; Höglinger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2016, Höglinger et al., 2014, and Höglinger et al., 2015.

claim: Site-directed variants of caged sphingosine enable release of bioactive lipid to specific organelles.
source: Alongside the recent development of site-directed variants of caged sphingosine, it has become possible to confine release of this bioactive lipid to specific organelles (Feng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Feng et al., 2018.

claim: Once triggered, caged lipid activity cannot be switched off and the decay of the lipid signal depends on its metabolic conversion.
source: However, once triggered, the activity cannot be switched off and the decay of the lipid signal depends on its metabolic conversion.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of caged compounds.

claim: Photoswitchable azobenzene-containing lipids allow the translation of optical stimuli into a reversible cellular response.
source: In this respect, photoswitchable azobenzene-containing lipids hold great promise by allowing the translation of optical stimuli into a reversible cellular response (Frank et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2016a; Frank et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frank et al., 2015, Frank et al., 2016a, and Frank et al., 2016b.

claim: Azobenzene-containing fatty acids are photoswitchable agonists of the vanilloid receptor 1.
source: In previous studies, we demonstrated the potency of azobenzene-containing fatty acids as photoswitchable agonists of the vanilloid receptor 1 (Frank et al., 2015), and found that photoswitchable DAGs enable light-mediated oscillations in protein kinase C activation (Frank et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank et al., 2015.

claim: Photoswitchable DAGs enable light-mediated oscillations in protein kinase C activation.
source: In previous studies, we demonstrated the potency of azobenzene-containing fatty acids as photoswitchable agonists of the vanilloid receptor 1 (Frank et al., 2015), and found that photoswitchable DAGs enable light-mediated oscillations in protein kinase C activation (Frank et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank et al., 2016a.

claim: Three azobenzene-containing ceramides (ACes) displayed light-dependent cycling between liquid-ordered (Lo) and liquid-disordered (Ld) domains when incorporated into phase-separated supported lipid bilayers.
source: We recently synthesized a set of azobenzene-containing ceramides (ACes) to exert optical control over the curvature of the N-acyl chain. All three ACes displayed a light-dependent cycling between liquid-ordered (Lo) and liquid-disordered (Ld) domains when incorporated into phase-separated supported lipid bilayers (SLBs), thus enabling dynamic manipulation of membrane structure and fluidity (Frank et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank et al., 2016b.

claim: ACes enable dynamic manipulation of membrane structure and fluidity.
source: We recently synthesized a set of azobenzene-containing ceramides (ACes) to exert optical control over the curvature of the N-acyl chain. All three ACes displayed a light-dependent cycling between liquid-ordered (Lo) and liquid-disordered (Ld) domains when incorporated into phase-separated supported lipid bilayers (SLBs), thus enabling dynamic manipulation of membrane structure and fluidity (Frank et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank et al., 2016b.

claim: Four clickable and azobenzene-containing ceramide analogues (caCer-1–4) were synthesized.
source: We designed and synthesized four clickable and azobenzene-containing ceramide analogues, caCer-1–4 (Figure 1a,b, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the chemical synthesis described in the methods and structures shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each caCer has an N-acyl chain possessing a terminal alkyne for click-derivatization with a fluorophore reporter.
source: Each caCer has an N-acyl chain possessing a terminal alkyne for click-derivatization with a fluorophore reporter.
evidence: This is a description of the chemical design of the caCers.

claim: caCer-1 is a clickable variant of ACe-1.
source: caCer-1 is a clickable variant of ACe-1 on which we reported earlier (Frank et al., 2016b) (Figure 1c), and carries the azobenzene photoswitch in its N-acyl chain with the diazene group mimicking a Δ9-double bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Frank et al., 2016b and the structure shown in Figure 1c.

claim: caCer-1 carries the azobenzene photoswitch in its N-acyl chain with the diazene group mimicking a Δ9-double bond.
source: caCer-1 is a clickable variant of ACe-1 on which we reported earlier (Frank et al., 2016b) (Figure 1c), and carries the azobenzene photoswitch in its N-acyl chain with the diazene group mimicking a Δ9-double bond.
evidence: This is a description of the chemical structure of caCer-1.

claim: caCer-2 has a shorter N-acyl chain with an azobenzene whose diazene group mimics a Δ6-double bond.
source: caCer-2 has a shorter N-acyl chain with an azobenzene whose diazene group mimics a Δ6-double bond.
evidence: This is a description of the chemical structure of caCer-2.

claim: caCer-1 and caCer-2 behave as standard azobenzenes.
source: UV-Vis spectroscopy revealed that both compounds behaved as standard azobenzenes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b.

claim: caCer-1 and caCer-2 exist in their thermally stable trans-configuration in the dark.
source: In the dark, they existed in their thermally stable trans-configuration, and could be isomerized to cis using UV-A (350–390 nm) illumination.
evidence: This is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data.

claim: caCer-1 and caCer-2 can be isomerized to cis using UV-A (350–390 nm) illumination.
source: In the dark, they existed in their thermally stable trans-configuration, and could be isomerized to cis using UV-A (350–390 nm) illumination.
evidence: This is based on UV-Vis spectroscopy data.

claim: The trans-isomer of caCer-1 and caCer-2 can be regenerated using blue (470 nm) light.
source: The trans-isomer could be regenerated using blue (470 nm) light (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: caCer-3 possesses a slightly red-shifted absorption spectrum, with a λmax at 365 nm.
source: UV-Vis spectroscopy revealed that the styrene caCer-3 possessed a slightly red-shifted absorption spectrum, with a λmax at 365 nm (Figure 1f) compared to about 335 nm for the rest of the caCers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by UV-Vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The trans to cis isomerization of caCer-3 is most efficient at 370 nm.
source: To determine the optimal photoswitching wavelength to generate cis-caCer-3, we continuously monitored the absorbance at 365 nm in solution and performed a wavelength scan between 350 to 410 nm. We found that the trans to cis isomerization of caCer-3 was most efficient at 370 nm, similar to the rest of the caCers and ACes (Frank et al., 2016b) (Figure 1g).
evidence: The claim is supported by wavelength scan data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: UV-A-induced isomerization of dark-adapted caCers to cis led to a rapid fluidification of the Lo domains in SLBs.
source: UV-A-induced isomerization of dark-adapted caCers to cis led to a rapid fluidification of the Lo domains, as indicated by the appearance of many small liquid-disordered (Ld) 'lakes' within the Lo domains, alongside an increase in the Ld/Lo area ratio.
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Isomerization of caCers to trans by blue light caused Ld lakes to shrink in size while surrounding Lo areas expanded.
source: On isomerization of caCers to trans by blue light, the Ld lakes shrunk in size while the surrounding Lo areas expanded, essentially occupying the same total area as in the original dark-adapted state.
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Light-induced effects on lipid domains were observed for both caCer-3 and caCer-4 and could be repeated over multiple cycles of UV-A and blue light illumination.
source: These light-induced effects on lipid domains were observed for both caCer-3 (Figure 2b, top) and caCer-4 (Figure 2b, bottom) and could be repeated over multiple cycles of UV-A and blue light illumination (Figure 2c, Figure 2—video 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM imaging data shown in Figure 2b, 2c and videos.

claim: Trans-isomers of caCer-3 and caCer-4 preferentially localize to cholesterol- and SM-rich Lo domains.
source: This indicates that, while trans-isomers of caCer-3 and caCer-4 preferentially localize to cholesterol- and SM-rich Lo domains, their cis-isomers favor association with more loosely packed lipids like DOPC.
evidence: This is inferred from the AFM imaging data showing domain preferences.

claim: Cis-isomers of caCer-3 and caCer-4 favor association with more loosely packed lipids like DOPC.
source: This indicates that, while trans-isomers of caCer-3 and caCer-4 preferentially localize to cholesterol- and SM-rich Lo domains, their cis-isomers favor association with more loosely packed lipids like DOPC.
evidence: This is inferred from the AFM imaging data showing domain preferences.

claim: All four caCers and cCer were converted into SM when incubated with lysates of SMS2-expressing yeast cells.
source: All four caCers and cCer were converted into SM when incubated with lysates of SMS2-expressing yeast cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: No conversion of caCers to SM was observed in lysates of control (EV) cells.
source: No conversion was observed in lysates of control (EV) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The cis (UV-A-irradiated) isomers of caCer-1 and caCer-2 were more efficiently metabolized by SMS2 than their corresponding trans (dark-adapted or blue-irradiated) isomers.
source: Strikingly, the cis (UV-A-irradiated) isomers of both caCer-1 and caCer-2 were more efficiently metabolized by SMS2 than their corresponding trans (dark-adapted or blue-irradiated) isomers.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: caCer-3 behaved similarly to caCer-1 and caCer-2, except that its blue irradiation led to a higher metabolic conversion by SMS2.
source: caCer-3 behaved similarly to caCer-1 and caCer-2, except that its blue irradiation led to a higher metabolic conversion by SMS2 (Figure 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The SMS2-mediated conversion of both caCer-4 and cCer was independent of light treatment.
source: In contrast, the SMS2-mediated conversion of both caCer-4 and cCer was independent of light treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Extending the incubation of SMS2-containing liposomes with dark-adapted caCer-1 under pulsed UV-A illumination led to a rise in the amount of SM produced.
source: Extending the incubation by 1 hr at 37°C in the dark resulted in only a minor increase in the amount of SM formed. However, extending the incubation under pulsed UV-A illumination led to a rise in the amount of SM produced.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Blue illumination did not enhance SM production from caCer-1 relative to dark-adapted liposomes.
source: In contrast, blue illumination did not enhance SM production relative to the dark-adapted liposomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: No light-induced fluctuations in SM production were observed with liposomes containing cCer.
source: No such light-induced fluctuations in SM production were observed with liposomes containing cCer.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Light-induced conformational changes in caCers have an acute impact on their metabolic conversion by SMS2 in both synthetic and cellular membranes.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that light-induced conformational changes in caCers have an acute impact on their metabolic conversion by SMS2 in both synthetic and cellular membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The efficiency by which both caCer-1 and caCer-3 were converted into SM increased instantly upon their isomerization to cis with UV-A light.
source: The efficiency by which both caCer-1 and caCer-3 were converted into SM increased instantly upon their isomerization to cis with UV-A light (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Isomerization of caCer-1 and caCer-3 back to trans with blue light resulted in an abrupt drop in the SM production rate.
source: Conversely, isomerization back to trans with blue light resulted in an abrupt drop in the SM production rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The block in SM production from caCers could be reversed again by illuminating the samples with UV-A light.
source: This block in SM production could be reversed again by illuminating the samples with UV-A light.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Light-induced changes in SM production rates were more pronounced for caCer-1 than for caCer-3.
source: In line with our foregoing data, the light-induced changes in SM production rates were more pronounced for caCer-1 than for caCer-3, and metabolic conversion of cCer into SM was not affected by UV-A or blue irradiation (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: Metabolic conversion of cCer into SM was not affected by UV-A or blue irradiation.
source: In line with our foregoing data, the light-induced changes in SM production rates were more pronounced for caCer-1 than for caCer-3, and metabolic conversion of cCer into SM was not affected by UV-A or blue irradiation (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: The bulk of SMS2-V5 resides at the plasma membrane in HeLa cells.
source: As expected, immunofluorescence microscopy revealed that the bulk of SMS2-V5 resides at the plasma membrane (Figure 5b,c) (Huitema et al., 2004; Tafesse et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5b,c and citations to Huitema et al., 2004 and Tafesse et al., 2007.

claim: The overall yield of SM produced in SMS2-overexpressing cells was at least threefold higher than that in control cells, regardless of the caCer isomer used.
source: The overall yield of SM produced in SMS2-overexpressing cells was at least threefold higher than that in control cells, regardless of the caCer isomer used (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5d-g.

claim: In both control and SMS2-overexpressing cells, cis-caCer-1 was more efficiently metabolized into SM than the trans-isomer.
source: However, in both control and SMS2-overexpressing cells, cis-caCer-1 was more efficiently metabolized into SM than the trans-isomer (Figure 5d,e), and similar results were obtained with caCer-3 (Figure 5f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Similar results to caCer-1 were obtained with caCer-3 in HeLa cells.
source: However, in both control and SMS2-overexpressing cells, cis-caCer-1 was more efficiently metabolized into SM than the trans-isomer (Figure 5d,e), and similar results were obtained with caCer-3 (Figure 5f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5f,g.

claim: Cells treated first with UV-A followed by blue-light produced similar amounts of SM as cells kept in the dark.
source: Cells treated first with UV-A followed by blue-light produced similar amounts of SM as cells kept in the dark (Figure 5h,i).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5h,i.

claim: Treating cells first with blue light followed by UV-A light caused a marked (3–5-fold) increase in SM production.
source: However, treating cells first with blue light followed by UV-A light caused a marked (3–5-fold) increase in SM production.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5h,i.

claim: Production of SM from cCer was not affected by light treatment in HeLa cells.
source: In contrast, production of SM from cCer was not affected by light treatment, demonstrating that UV-A irradiation itself did not affect SM-production in HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5h,i.

claim: UV-A irradiation itself did not affect SM-production in HeLa cells.
source: In contrast, production of SM from cCer was not affected by light treatment, demonstrating that UV-A irradiation itself did not affect SM-production in HeLa cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment with cCer.

claim: caCers are suitable as photoswitchable substrates for manipulating SM biosynthesis in living cells with the temporal precision of light.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate the suitability of caCers as photoswitchable substrates for manipulating SM biosynthesis in living cells with the temporal precision of light.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in HeLa cells.

claim: GCS is a Golgi-resident enzyme that generates glucosylceramide (GlcCer) by transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to ceramide.
source: We employed a yeast strain expressing human glucosylceramide synthase (GCS; Figure 6a), a Golgi-resident enzyme structurally unrelated to SMS2 that generates glucosylceramide (GlcCer) by transferring glucose from UDP-glucose to ceramide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GCS function.

claim: UV-A-irradiated caCer-1 was converted to GlcCer when incubated with lysates of GCS-expressing yeast cells in the presence of UDP-glucose.
source: When incubated with lysates of GCS-expressing yeast cells in the presence of UDP-glucose, UV-A-irradiated caCer-1 was converted to GlcCer (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: No GlcCer was formed when UDP-glucose was omitted or when yeast lysates that lack GCS were used.
source: No GlcCer was formed when UDP-glucose was omitted or when yeast lysates that lack GCS were used.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Metabolic conversion of caCer-1 by GCS was light sensitive, with the cis-isomers being more readily converted to GlcCer than the trans-isomers.
source: Analogous to our results with SMS2, metabolic conversion of caCer-1 by GCS was light sensitive, with the cis-isomers being more readily converted to GlcCer than the trans-isomers (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6c,d.

claim: Subjecting trans-caCer-1-containing lysates to an 'off-ON' switching regime (blue then UV-A) enabled GlcCer production.
source: Subjecting trans-caCer-1-containing lysates to an 'off-ON' switching regime (blue then UV-A) enabled GlcCer production (Figure 6e).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Keeping the lysates in the dark or subjecting them to an 'on-OFF' switching regime (UV-A then blue) blocked GlcCer production.
source: In contrast, keeping the lysates in the dark or subjecting them to an 'on-OFF' switching regime (UV-A then blue) blocked GlcCer production.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In lysates containing cCer, GlcCer production was independent of light.
source: In lysates containing cCer, GlcCer production was independent of light (Figure 6c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6c-e.

claim: GlcCer production from caCer-1 was strongly stimulated by UV-A illumination in cell-free produced GCS proteoliposomes.
source: While only small amounts of GlcCer were formed when caCer-1-containing proteoliposomes were kept in the dark, GlcCer production was strongly stimulated by UV-A illumination (Figure 6g).
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: GlcCer production in cCer-containing proteoliposomes was insensitive to UV-A illumination.
source: In contrast, GlcCer production in cCer-containing proteoliposomes was insensitive to UV-A illumination.
evidence: The claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: The application of caCers as light-sensitive substrates is not restricted to one particular class of ceramide metabolic enzymes.
source: Importantly, these results demonstrate that the application of caCers as light-sensitive substrates is not restricted to one particular class of ceramide metabolic enzymes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing both SMS2 and GCS can be controlled with caCers.

claim: Cis-isomers of caCer-1, caCer-2 and caCer-3 are more readily metabolized by SMS2 than their corresponding trans-isomers.
source: Using synthetic and cellular membrane systems as experimental models, we found that cis-isomers of caCer-1, caCer-2 and caCer-3 are more readily metabolized by SMS2 than their corresponding trans-isomers.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from Figures 3-5.

claim: SM synthases are relatively tolerant toward structural deviations in the ceramide backbone and readily metabolize ceramide analogous with distinct functional groups in the sphingoid base or N-acyl chain.
source: However, this theory conflicts with the finding that SM synthases are relatively tolerant toward structural deviations in the ceramide backbone and readily metabolize ceramide analogous with distinct functional groups in the sphingoid base or N-acyl chain (Koval and Pagano, 1991; Huitema et al., 2004; Haberkant et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koval and Pagano, 1991, Huitema et al., 2004, and Haberkant et al., 2016.

claim: Trans-caCers form tightly packed clusters due to favorable intermolecular stacking interactions among the flat trans-azobenzene groups.
source: According to this model, trans-caCers form tightly packed clusters due to favorable intermolecular stacking interactions among the flat trans-azobenzene groups, thereby reducing their availability for enzymatic conversion.
evidence: This is a hypothetical model proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: On isomerization to cis, the kinked caCer molecules become dispersed throughout the membrane, making them more accessible for enzymatic conversion.
source: On isomerization to cis, the kinked caCer molecules become dispersed throughout the membrane, making them more accessible for enzymatic conversion.
evidence: This is a hypothetical model proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Trans-caCers preferentially localize in liquid-ordered (Lo) domains in model bilayers.
source: This idea is supported by our finding that trans-caCers preferentially localize in liquid-ordered (Lo) domains in model bilayers (Figure 2) (Frank et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 2 and citation to Frank et al., 2016b.

claim: caCer-4 forms an exception, as its isomerization to trans promotes association with Lo domains without having an obvious impact on SM biosynthesis.
source: caCer-4 forms an exception, as its isomerization to trans promotes association with Lo domains without having an obvious impact on SM biosynthesis.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: caCers offer superior temporal resolution for manipulating sphingolipid levels compared to traditional pulse-chase approaches.
source: This property enabled us to generate time-resolved pulses of SM synthesis at the plasma membrane of living cells. In comparison to traditional pulse-chase approaches, our method offers superior temporal resolution for manipulating sphingolipid levels, and could be combined with patterned illumination to generate controlled sphingolipid pulses in subpopulations of cells or in subcellular organelles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison to existing methods.

claim: caCers could be combined with patterned illumination to generate controlled sphingolipid pulses in subpopulations of cells or in subcellular organelles.
source: This property enabled us to generate time-resolved pulses of SM synthesis at the plasma membrane of living cells. In comparison to traditional pulse-chase approaches, our method offers superior temporal resolution for manipulating sphingolipid levels, and could be combined with patterned illumination to generate controlled sphingolipid pulses in subpopulations of cells or in subcellular organelles.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: caCers may find use in dissecting the causal roles of ceramides in apoptosis, as tumor suppressors, and as antagonists of insulin signaling.
source: Accordingly, caCers may find use in dissecting the causal roles of ceramides in apoptosis, as tumor suppressors, and as antagonists of insulin signaling (Hannun and Obeid, 2018; Jain et al., 2017; Park et al., 2016; Meikle and Summers, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Light-induced changes in lateral packing may be a previously unnoted characteristic of other azobenzene-containing signaling lipids like DAGs.
source: In fact, light-induced changes in lateral packing may be a previously unnoted characteristic of other azobenzene-containing signaling lipids like DAGs, where the cis-isomers correspond to the bioactive form (Frank et al., 2016a; Leinders-Zufall et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the current findings and citations to related work.

claim: Application of caCers in living cells is hampered by their relatively poor aqueous solubility.
source: Application of caCers in living cells is hampered by their relatively poor aqueous solubility.
evidence: This is an observation about a limitation of the compounds.

claim: The development of photoswitchable sphingoid bases may provide a way to circumvent limitations associated with the relative inefficient uptake of caCers by cells.
source: However, the development of photoswitchable sphingoid bases may provide a way to circumvent limitations associated with the relative inefficient uptake of caCers by cells, thus expanding opportunities for manipulating the metabolic fate and signaling activity of sphingolipids by light.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future developments.

claim: Ceramides are the precursors of a large collection of complex sphingolipids with critical roles in sustaining mechanical stability, molecular sorting, cell signaling, migration and adhesion.
source: Ceramides are the precursors of a large collection of complex sphingolipids with critical roles in sustaining mechanical stability, molecular sorting, cell signaling, migration and adhesion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ceramide function.

claim: caCers provide attractive scaffolds for creating a new toolbox of photoswitchable sphingolipids to enable optical control over a wide array of sphingolipid-mediated cellular processes.
source: Consequently, caCers provide attractive scaffolds for creating a new toolbox of photoswitchable sphingolipids to enable optical control over a wide array of sphingolipid-mediated cellular processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applications of the technology.

claim: Confocal fluorescence imaging of SLBs from lipid mixtures containing the dark-adapted trans-caCers revealed a clear phase separation.
source: Confocal fluorescence imaging of SLBs from lipid mixtures containing the dark-adapted trans-caCers revealed a clear phase separation, with liquid-ordered (Lo) domains appearing as dark regions (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Liquid-ordered (Lo) domains in SLBs rested approximately 1 nm above the Ld phase.
source: Imaging of the SLBs by AFM confirmed the formation of Lo domains, which rested approximately 1 nm above the Ld phase (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: HeLa cells were mycoplasma free.
source: HeLa cells were mycoplasma free.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality control of the cell line used.
